description: Every finding this product can raise. One rule produces zero or more findings, each attached to a named component with the evidence that triggered it. Change what the product reports here, not in code. A rule with no 'detection' is not implemented and the contract integrity test fails on it, which is deliberate: a catalogue that lists aspirations reads identically to one that lists capabilities.

principles.doNotReimplementTheChecker: The Power Apps checker service already does static analysis of JavaScript, plugins and canvas apps, its rules move, and Microsoft maintains them. This product calls it and folds the results in under their own rule ids rather than writing a second, worse, staler version. Rules declared here are the ones the checker does not have: cross component debt, lifecycle, usage, sprawl and solution hygiene.
principles.everyFindingNamesARecord: A finding says 'this workflow, on this table, last run never'. Not 'classic workflows are dated'. The second one is a sentence a consultant could have written without the tool, and nobody pays for it.
principles.evidenceTravels: The evidence that triggered a rule is carried with the finding all the way into the report and the work item. A recommendation somebody cannot check is a recommendation somebody will not act on.
principles.severityIsAboutConsequence: Not about how annoying it is. Critical means something is broken or unsafe now. High means it will break or cost money on a known horizon. Medium and low are judgement and hygiene.
principles.noFindingWithoutAReachableSource: A rule whose evidence source the current extraction mode cannot reach is reported as not assessed, per rule, in the run header. It is never silently skipped and never reported as passing.

severities.critical: Broken or unsafe now. A failing integration, an unrestricted privilege, a component that cannot be deployed.
severities.high: Will cost money or break on a known horizon. A removed component still present, a deprecated API in use, a flow failing a fifth of the time.
severities.medium: Real debt with no deadline. Dated components, missing error handling, sprawl.
severities.low: Hygiene. Naming, unused metadata, documentation gaps.
severities.info: Context rather than a problem. Counted, reported, never estimated.

categories.name: Lifecycle and deprecation
categories.description: Components Microsoft has removed, deprecated or stopped investing in.

categories.name: Modernisation
categories.description: Something that works and has a better answer now. The category a client actually wants and the one most likely to be oversold, so every rule here carries a reason to leave it alone as well.

categories.name: Build quality
categories.description: How well the thing that exists was built. Error handling, naming, structure.

categories.name: Architecture
categories.description: Whether logic sits where logic should sit. The low code ratio lives here.

categories.name: ALM and solution hygiene
categories.description: Whether this can be moved between environments without a person remembering something.

categories.name: Governance
categories.description: Ownership, sprawl, orphaned components, licensing exposure.

categories.name: Performance
categories.description: Things that are slow now or will be at volume.

categories.name: Security
categories.description: Privilege, secrets and exposure. Not a penetration test and does not pretend to be.

categories.name: Operability
categories.description: Whether anybody would find out when it breaks.

checkerIntegration.rulesetIdNote: Resolved at run time from the ruleset endpoint rather than hard coded, so rules Microsoft adds arrive without a release here. The AppSource Certification ruleset is offered as an option for ISV work and is not the default: it is stricter in ways that produce noise on a client estate.

categoryMapping.description: Checker results arrive with their own categories. They are mapped onto the categories above so one report does not have two vocabularies, and the original checker category and rule id travel with the finding.

checkerIntegration.failureHandling: A checker job that fails or times out marks every checker sourced rule as not assessed for that run. The rest of the analysis completes. A report that silently omits the checker half while looking complete is the failure mode to avoid here.

rules.name: Dialog still present
rules.detection: Any dialog record in the solution, in any state.
rules.why: Dialogs were removed in 2020. One sitting here means nobody has audited this solution in five years, which is worth knowing before reading any other number in this report.
rules.recommendation: Delete it. If the process it described still matters, it is being done by hand now and nobody has noticed.

rules.name: Deprecated client API in a web resource
rules.detection: Delegated to the checker. Folded in under the checker's own rule id, with this rule as the parent for grouping and estimating.
rules.why: Removed client APIs fail at run time, on a form, in front of a user, with no build to catch it first.
rules.recommendation: Replace each call with its documented successor. The checker names the replacement.
rules.falsePositive: A library shipped by a third party solution is not yours to fix. Findings on managed web resources are reported separately and not estimated.

rules.name: Classic workflow carrying live logic
rules.detection: Workflow in an activated state, with at least one execution in the last thirty days or, where runtime evidence is unavailable, activated at all.
rules.why: Not deprecated, and the designer has had no investment in years. The cost is that the people who can maintain it are becoming the people who remember it.
rules.recommendation: Replace when you are in the component for another reason. A migration project of its own is rarely worth funding on this finding alone, and a report that says otherwise is overselling.
rules.falsePositive: A real time workflow that rolls back a transaction has no like for like replacement in Power Automate. Check the mode before recommending anything.

rules.name: Classic workflow activated and never running
rules.detection: Workflow activated, zero executions in ninety days, and a trigger that would have fired given the row volume on its table.
rules.why: Either it is dead and should go, or it should have run and did not, which is worse.
rules.recommendation: Confirm which of the two it is before deleting anything.

rules.name: Custom workflow activity pinning a classic workflow
rules.detection: A custom workflow activity referenced by at least one activated workflow.
rules.why: The workflow cannot be replaced until the code has somewhere to go, so this is the finding that sets the order of the modernisation backlog.
rules.recommendation: Move the logic to a custom API or a plugin first, then replace the workflow.

rules.name: RDL report
rules.detection: Any report of type RDL in the solution.
rules.why: Supported, static, and where reporting stopped. Each one is a Power BI candidate with a real hours cost, which is why they are listed individually rather than summarised.
rules.recommendation: Inventory, then decide per report. A report nobody has run in a year is a deletion, not a migration.

rules.name: Dataflow in the estate
rules.detection: Any dataflow in the environment, in or out of a solution.
rules.why: No CLI support and no catalogue API, so a dataflow does not travel through an ALM pipeline and does not appear in most governance tooling. It also consumes Dataverse capacity in a way that surfaces as a bill rather than as an alert.
rules.recommendation: Decide whether it is load bearing. If it is, rebuild it somewhere that can be versioned.

rules.name: One table with logic in more than three places
rules.detection: A single table targeted by components from more than three of: plugin step, classic workflow, cloud flow, business rule, low code plugin, calculated or formula column, client script.
rules.why: This is the finding that explains why a change on that table takes three weeks and breaks something unrelated. Nobody can hold the order of execution in their head, and no document describes it.
rules.recommendation: Map what fires on create and on update, in order, and consolidate. The map is most of the value even if nothing is consolidated.

rules.name: Script doing what a business rule does
rules.detection: A form script whose only operations are setVisible, setDisabled, setRequiredLevel and getValue comparisons, with no network call and no unsupported API.
rules.why: Code that has to be deployed to do something configuration does, which means a maker has to raise a ticket to change a field label's behaviour.
rules.recommendation: Replace with a business rule, entity scoped if the same validation needs to hold server side.
rules.falsePositive: Business rules cannot do everything a script can. Anything touching a subgrid, a tab or a quick view form stays as a script.

rules.name: Low code to high code ratio
rules.detection: Computed per the ratioRules in component-model.json, per solution and across the analysed set.
rules.why: A number the client asked for, which means it will be quoted without its definition. The definition travels with it in every export for that reason.
rules.recommendation: Read it next to the domain breakdown. A high pro code share in the integration domain is normal. The same share in the logic domain is a finding.

rules.name: Logic outside the platform with no documented owner
rules.detection: A service endpoint or custom connector pointing at a host outside the Dataverse and Microsoft 365 domains.
rules.why: A solution can look clean while most of its behaviour sits in an Azure Function nobody in the room has seen. This finding puts a floor under how much of that there is.
rules.recommendation: Name an owner and a repository for each one. The report cannot tell you what is behind the URL.

rules.name: Cloud flow with no failure path
rules.detection: A flow with more than five actions, no scope configured to run after a failure, and no terminate with a failed status.
rules.why: It fails silently. The run history knows, and the run history is not something anybody reads unprompted.
rules.recommendation: Wrap the body in a scope with a configure run after handler that reports the failure somewhere a person looks.

rules.name: Cloud flow failing regularly
rules.detection: Failure rate above ten percent over thirty days, with at least twenty runs.
rules.why: Something is broken now. Whether anybody has noticed is a separate question and usually has the same answer.
rules.recommendation: Read the last failure before estimating anything. A flow failing on a data condition is a different job from one failing on an expired connection.

rules.name: Cloud flow too large to reason about
rules.detection: More than forty actions, or nesting deeper than four levels.
rules.why: Low code by construction and unmaintainable in practice. Nobody changes one of these confidently, so eventually nobody changes it at all.
rules.recommendation: Split into child flows along the steps a person would describe out loud.

rules.name: Canvas app with delegation warnings
rules.detection: Delegation warnings reported by the checker, weighted by the row count of the table behind the data source.
rules.why: It works in test with two hundred rows and returns wrong answers in production with fifty thousand. Wrong answers, not slow ones, which is why this is high rather than medium.
rules.recommendation: Fix the ones over a table with real volume first. A delegation warning over a lookup table of twelve rows is noise.

rules.name: Plugin with no tracing
rules.detection: Delegated to the checker where it covers this, plus absence of any trace log entry over thirty days for a step that executed.
rules.why: When it throws in production there is nothing to read.
rules.recommendation: Add tracing at the entry and exit of each handler and at every branch that can throw.

rules.name: Plugin assembly not in sandbox isolation
rules.detection: isolationMode is none, or sourceType is anything other than database.
rules.why: It cannot be deployed to an online environment and it cannot be moved. This is usually a finding about where the solution came from rather than about the code.
rules.recommendation: Rebuild against sandbox isolation. Expect to find something in there that needs full trust and to have a longer conversation about it.

rules.name: Form loading more script than it needs
rules.detection: More than four script libraries registered on a form, or a library over one hundred kilobytes registered on more than five forms.
rules.why: Form load time is the thing users complain about and the thing nobody measures.
rules.recommendation: Register libraries where they are used rather than everywhere, and check whether the large one is a framework that could be a platform library instead.

rules.name: Unmanaged customisation in a production environment
rules.detection: Unmanaged components in an environment the connection is marked as production, outside the default solution exclusion list.
rules.why: There is no pipeline. Whatever is here was made here, and the environment is the source of truth, which means there is no rollback and no review.
rules.recommendation: This is not a component finding. It is a delivery finding and it outranks everything else in the report.

rules.name: Components living in the default solution
rules.detection: Custom components whose only solution membership is the default solution.
rules.why: They do not travel. Somebody will find out when the next deployment is missing a column.
rules.recommendation: Move each one into a named solution with a publisher prefix that means something.

rules.name: More than one publisher prefix in one solution
rules.detection: Custom components in a solution carrying two or more distinct publisher prefixes, excluding managed dependencies.
rules.why: Usually means two teams, or one team and a consultancy, building in the same place without agreeing anything. Harmless on its own and a reliable signal of something else.
rules.recommendation: Leave existing components alone. Renaming a prefix is not a thing you can do. Agree the prefix for new work.

rules.name: Flow with an embedded connection rather than a reference
rules.detection: A flow whose definition carries a connection without a corresponding connection reference in the solution.
rules.why: It will import and it will not run, and the error will be reported by whoever tested the wrong thing first.
rules.recommendation: Add a connection reference per connector and repoint the flow.

rules.name: Environment specific value hard coded
rules.detection: A URL, a GUID matching a record in a configuration table, or an email domain, appearing literally in a definition where an environment variable exists in the solution or could.
rules.why: The solution imports cleanly into test and points at production.
rules.recommendation: Replace with an environment variable. Leave the default value empty rather than setting it to the development value.
rules.falsePositive: A Microsoft service URL is not an environment specific value. The detection excludes the documented Microsoft domain list.

rules.name: Environment variable shipping a default value
rules.detection: An environment variable with a default value and no current value, in a solution intended to be exported as managed.
rules.why: The default travels into the target environment and looks like a deliberate setting. Nobody changes it because nothing says it needs changing.
rules.recommendation: Ship the definition, set the value per environment in the pipeline.

rules.name: Column on no form and no view
rules.detection: A custom column referenced by no form, no view, no flow, no plugin registration filtering attribute and no calculated column.
rules.why: The most common finding in this product by volume, and the one to be most careful with. A column with no interface reference is often written by an integration.
rules.recommendation: Check the API usage before proposing a deletion. Report the count prominently and the individual deletions cautiously.
rules.falsePositive: Integrations write to columns no form shows. This rule cannot see an integration, and its finding is a question rather than a recommendation.

rules.name: Security role held by nobody
rules.detection: A custom security role with no users and no teams assigned.
rules.why: Every one of these is a decision somebody made and nobody recorded. They also make the role picker unusable, which is how people end up assigning System Administrator.
rules.recommendation: Delete, after checking it is not assigned by a provisioning process that runs monthly.

rules.name: Custom role with organisation level write
rules.detection: A custom role granting write, delete or share at organisation level on a table holding personal data or financial data, per the table classification in the run configuration.
rules.why: Usually granted to make something work during a go live and never narrowed afterwards.
rules.recommendation: Narrow to business unit or user level and test what breaks. Something will.

rules.name: Secret in a component definition
rules.detection: A string matching a key, token or connection string shape in a definition that is exported, versioned and readable by anybody with maker access.
rules.why: It is in the solution file, which means it is in source control, which means rotating it is the smallest part of the job.
rules.recommendation: Rotate first, then move to Key Vault through an environment variable. In that order.

rules.name: Premium connector in use
rules.detection: Any connection reference to a connector on the premium list.
rules.why: A licensing conversation, not a technical one. Reported as information because this product cannot see what licences the tenant holds and should not guess.
rules.recommendation: Check the finding against the licences in place before drawing a conclusion.

rules.name: Component owned by a disabled user
rules.detection: Owner is a user in a disabled state, or a user absent from the directory.
rules.why: A flow owned by somebody who left runs on their connections until those expire, and then it stops, and nobody knows why.
rules.recommendation: Reassign to a service principal or a group owned solution. Reassigning to another person recreates the problem with a later date on it.

rules.name: Synchronous plugin running long
rules.detection: A synchronous step with an average execution above two thousand milliseconds over thirty days.
rules.why: It is inside the user's save. Everything above two seconds is felt.
rules.recommendation: Move what does not need to be in the transaction out of it.

rules.name: Update step with no filtering attributes
rules.detection: A step registered on Update with an empty filtering attribute list.
rules.why: It runs on every change to every column on that table, including the ones written by other plugins, which is also how recursion starts.
rules.recommendation: List the columns the handler actually reads.

rules.name: View joining too much
rules.detection: More than five linked entities, or more than twenty columns, on a view set as a default.
rules.why: It is the first thing every user of that table loads.
rules.recommendation: Trim the default view. Keep the wide one as a named alternative.

rules.name: No failure alerting anywhere in the solution
rules.detection: No component in the analysed set sends a failure notification: no flow posting to a channel or mailbox on a failure path, no service endpoint on an error, no Application Insights key configured on the environment.
rules.why: Everything above about failure rates assumes somebody finds out. This rule checks that assumption once, at the solution level, rather than repeating it per component.
rules.recommendation: One failure path that reaches a person beats per component handling that reaches a run history.

rules.name: Same components present in every environment as unmanaged
rules.detection: Where more than one environment is connected, the same solution present unmanaged in all of them with diverging versions.
rules.why: There is no promotion path, there is copying. The versions have already diverged, which is why the finding is critical rather than high.
rules.recommendation: Pick the environment that is closest to right and make it the source. This is a project rather than a fix.

rules.name: Inconsistent naming across a solution
rules.detection: More than two distinct casing or separator conventions in the display names of one component type within one solution.
rules.why: Cosmetic, cheap to report and consistently the thing a client points at first in a workshop. It is also a proxy for how many people have built here without a standard.
rules.recommendation: Agree a convention for new work. Renaming existing components is rarely worth the regression risk.

rules.name: Component with no description
rules.detection: Empty description on a custom component.
rules.why: The cost lands on whoever inherits this, which on a consultancy engagement is the client.
rules.recommendation: Fill in descriptions as part of whatever work touches the component. A separate description backlog never gets done.

roadmap.description: Where a finding sits on the roadmap grid. Two axes and three bands, taken from the assessment format this product automates. Placement is per rule rather than per finding, because the axis a finding sits on is a property of the kind of problem rather than of the component.

row.business: Visible to the business. Someone outside IT notices when it is fixed.
row.process: Organisation and process. Nobody outside IT notices directly, and everything above it is slower without it.

column.architecture: How the solution is shaped. Changing it means changing decisions.
column.technology: What it is built on. Changing it means changing components.

bands.unclutter: Remove, consolidate, delete. Buys capacity rather than capability, and it is where most of the findings in a mature estate sit.
bands.accelerate: Make the existing thing faster or safer to change. Pipelines, error handling, references, privilege.
bands.innovate: New capability. Almost nothing an analyser finds belongs here, and a report claiming otherwise is selling.

roadmap.honesty: Most findings land in unclutter. That is the correct shape for a technical debt assessment, and a roadmap where everything lands in innovate has been drawn to please somebody rather than to describe an estate.
